title: {{NAME}} and the Map of Invisible Roads
moral: The truest guides are not those who know every path, but those who listen hard enough to let the lost lead the way.

pages.content: The Whispering Wood was the kind of forest that rearranged itself when no one was paying attention, not maliciously, simply out of habit, the way some people rearrange the furniture because they find it interesting. Paths that existed on Tuesday were gone by Thursday, replaced by streams that had not been there before and clearings full of flowers that bloomed only in specific shades of blue. {{NAME}} had been walking for twenty minutes and was, by any honest accounting, thoroughly lost. His chestnut boots were damp with stream-crossings. His teal coat was festooned with small burrs. But he was not frightened. He was interested, which is a much more useful thing to be when you are lost. From a mossy branch directly above his head, something small cleared its throat with precise and official authority. {{NAME}} looked up. A fairy perched there, no bigger than his fist, with wings like lacework and the expression of someone who has been supervising a difficult situation for longer than is strictly reasonable.

pages.content: The fairy's name was Moss, and she was the wood's official path-keeper, a title that had become considerably more stressful recently because Princess Fen had gone missing. Princess Fen was eleven years old, had arrived in the wood three days ago following a rumour about a flower that granted perfect musical pitch, and had not been seen since. The wood had been rearranging itself especially energetically since her arrival, which Moss considered suspicious and possibly related. Fen's animal companions, a pair of enormously sensible otters named Pip and Chalk, had been searching without pause and were now sitting on a root nearby, their dark eyes red-rimmed with worry, their sleek heads drooping. Moss briefed {{NAME}} with the speed and efficiency of someone who has been waiting for a competent newcomer. When she finished, {{NAME}} crouched beside the otters. He asked them not where they had searched, but where Fen had been going. Where she had wanted to go. Pip and Chalk exchanged a look. Then Chalk tapped the ground once with a small flat paw, very precisely.

pages.content: Following an otter who knows where it is going is like following a river, all purpose and no hesitation. Chalk ran with his nose low to the ground and Pip shadowed every turn, and {{NAME}} ran after them with Moss buzzing at his left ear, narrating obstacles he had already seen. The wood did try to rearrange itself around them, streams nudging in from the left, new trees crowding the path's edge, but the otters were faster than the forest's patience and they kept the thread. They found Fen in a glade so blue it looked like the inside of a held breath. She sat on a root that arched over a small still pond, her feet dangling, her dark hair loose, a notebook open in her lap. She was not hurt. She was singing, very softly, to a circle of animals that had gathered to listen: two deer, a hedgehog, a family of wrens. The flowers around her were the ones she had been looking for, and they were trembling slightly, as if the music were the thing they had been waiting for in order to bloom properly. Fen looked up and saw {{NAME}}, and her expression was not embarrassed. It was simply glad.

pages.content: But the glade was not finished. As Fen rose to greet them, the still pond surface stirred and something rose from it: not a monster, not a threat, but a mirror. A flat disc of silver water lifting itself upright, showing not the glade but somewhere else, a place where enormous trees had toppled in a storm, blocking a stream and flooding a badger sett whose inhabitants were clustered on a nearby bank, anxious and wet. The pond was showing them a problem. The wood, it seemed, had not been rearranging itself out of habit. It had been herding Fen here deliberately, because Fen had the notebook and the knowledge and the song that could help. {{NAME}} looked at Fen. Fen looked at her notebook. She sang three specific notes, very clearly, and the otters plunged into the pool. Where they emerged was a different place entirely, and {{NAME}} followed without hesitation, teal coat streaming, Moss a bright spark at his shoulder. Behind him, the glade blazed fully into blue bloom, every flower at once, and even the fish in the pond turned to watch.

pages.content: The badgers were safe before the last light left the forest, reunited with their sett, the fallen trees shifted by a collective effort of the otters, {{NAME}}'s considerable determination, and Fen directing from her notebook with the particular focus of someone who has finally found what she was supposed to be doing. Moss oversaw everything from the highest available branch and made notes in a very small book that she kept in her left wing. By the time they all found a warm, dry clearing to rest in, the wood had settled around them with the comfortable stillness of a forest that has got what it wanted. Fen sang quietly to the badger cubs, who fell asleep in a pile of damp grey fur. {{NAME}} lay in the soft moss with Pip and Chalk warm against his sides, heavier than they looked. His eyes refused to stay open. The wood breathed slowly around him, rearranging itself not at all. He slept deeply and well. But the silver pool was still there, still glowing in the glade, and whatever it showed next had not yet been seen.
